title: ACT English Practice Test 2
instructions: Each passage has underlined portions. Choose the best alternative (or NO CHANGE). Some questions ask about the passage as a whole.

passages.title: The Renaissance and Its Impact on European Thought
passages.text: The Renaissance, which began in Italy during the 14th century, represented [1] a profound shift in European intellectual and cultural life. This period marked [2] the transition from medieval to modern thought, emphasizing [3] humanistic values, scientific inquiry, and artistic innovation. Unlike the Middle Ages, [4] which focused on religious doctrine and the afterlife, Renaissance thinkers valued the [5] classical wisdom of ancient Greece and Rome. The rediscovery of classical texts [6] during this era proved transformative for philosophy, literature, and science. Scholars and artists [7] drew inspiration from these ancient sources to reimagine their contemporary world. [8] The printing press, invented by Johannes Gutenberg around 1440, revolutionized [9] the dissemination of knowledge and made education more accessible to the general population. [10] Before this innovation, books were rare, expensive, and laboriously copied by hand. [11] The Renaissance witnessed the rise of influential figures such as Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and Niccolò Machiavelli, [12] each of whom [13] contributed groundbreaking ideas to art, science, and political philosophy. Leonardo's anatomical drawings, based on [14] careful observation and dissection, advanced medical knowledge centuries ahead of the formal scientific method. [15] Michelangelo's artistic mastery demonstrated [16] that human creativity could achieve divine-like beauty, challenging medieval assumptions about art's purpose. [17] In the political sphere, Machiavelli's pragmatic approach to governance [18] offered an alternative to the idealistic theories that had dominated medieval political thought. [19] The Renaissance emphasis on individual achievement [20] transformed education, encouraging students to develop their talents and express their unique perspectives. [21] Despite its remarkable achievements, the Renaissance also contained [22] contradictions and conflicts that would shape European history for centuries to come.

passages.title: Biodiversity in Tropical Rainforests
passages.text: Tropical rainforests cover only about six percent of Earth's land surface, yet [23] they harbor more than half of the planet's known species. [24] This extraordinary concentration of biodiversity [25] results from the region's warm temperature, high rainfall, and complex ecosystem structure. [26] The rainforest canopy creates multiple layers of habitat, [27] allowing countless organisms to coexist in the same geographic area. [28] Despite their ecological importance, rainforests face unprecedented threats from deforestation. [29] Logging operations, agricultural expansion, and urban development are destroying [30] these vital ecosystems at an alarming rate, eliminating species before [31] scientists have even identified them. [32] The loss of rainforest habitat has profound consequences for global biodiversity, climate regulation, [33] and human communities that depend on the forest for survival. [34] Indigenous peoples have inhabited [35] and managed rainforests sustainably for thousands of years, [36] developing deep knowledge of forest ecology and plant properties. [37] Many pharmaceutical compounds derived from rainforest plants [38] have revolutionized [39] modern medicine, treating diseases from malaria to cancer. [40] The destruction of rainforests means the loss of potential medical discoveries [41] that could benefit humanity for generations to come. [42] Conservation efforts must balance [43] economic pressures with environmental protection, recognizing that rainforest preservation [44] is essential for maintaining global biodiversity and addressing climate change. [45] Protected reserves and sustainable harvesting practices [46] offer hope for preserving rainforests while respecting the rights and needs [47] of indigenous communities. [48] International cooperation and funding [49] are crucial for implementing these conservation strategies effectively. [50] The urgency of rainforest conservation cannot be overstated, [51] as we face a critical window of opportunity to reverse deforestation trends [52] and protect these irreplaceable ecosystems for future generations. [53]

passages.title: The Evolution of the Internet
passages.text: The Internet emerged from military research conducted [54] during the Cold War, when the U.S. Department of Defense funded [55] the development of a decentralized communication network resistant [56] to nuclear attack. [57] ARPANET, the precursor to the modern Internet, [58] was first established in 1969 and connected computer networks at [59] universities and research institutions across the United States. [60] The development of key technologies, including the TCP/IP protocol and the World Wide [61] Web, transformed ARPANET from a specialized research network into a global communication platform. [62] Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989, [63] creating a system for organizing and displaying information across interconnected computers. [64] His innovation made the Internet accessible to the general public, [65] revolutionizing how people communicate, work, and access information. [66] In the 1990s, the proliferation of personal computers and commercial Internet service providers [67] accelerated the adoption of Internet technology among households and businesses. [68] The rise of the World Wide Web led to [69] the emergence of websites, online commerce, and digital communities that [70] transformed society in unprecedented ways. [71] Email became the dominant mode of business communication, [72] replacing traditional correspondence and making information exchange instantaneous. [73] As the Internet grew, concerns about security, [74] privacy, and digital divide between wealthy and developing nations [75] became increasingly pressing issues. [76] Major technological advances, including the development of mobile Internet, social media platforms, [77] and cloud computing, [78] continued to reshape how we work, communicate, and consume information. [79] Today, the Internet has become so integrated into daily life [80] that it is difficult to imagine functioning in contemporary society without digital connectivity. [81] Yet, [82] ongoing challenges such as cybersecurity threats, digital addiction, and misinformation [83] require constant innovation and vigilance. [84] The future of the Internet [85] depends on developing new technologies while addressing the social and ethical implications [86] of ubiquitous digital connectivity. [87]

passages.title: The Importance of Emotional Intelligence in Leadership
passages.text: Emotional intelligence, defined as the ability to recognize, understand, and manage [88] emotions in oneself and others, has emerged as a critical component [89] of effective leadership in contemporary organizations. [90] Research demonstrates that leaders [91] with high emotional intelligence are better equipped to [92] navigate complex interpersonal situations and make decisions that benefit their organizations. [93] Unlike traditional measures of intelligence, which focus on cognitive abilities, [94] emotional intelligence encompasses self-awareness, empathy, and social skills. [94] Leaders with strong self-awareness [95] understand their own emotions and how [96] these emotions influence their behavior and decision-making. [97] This awareness enables them to respond [98] thoughtfully to challenges rather than reacting impulsively. [99] Empathy, another crucial component of emotional intelligence, [100] allows leaders to understand and respect diverse [101] perspectives and the needs of their team members. [102] Leaders who practice active listening [103] and show genuine concern for their employees [104] foster stronger relationships and higher morale. [105] Social skills, including communication, conflict resolution, [106] and collaboration, are enhanced by emotional intelligence. [107] Leaders with well-developed social skills [108] can build stronger teams and inspire greater loyalty [109] and commitment from their employees. [109] Research studies have shown [110] that organizations led by emotionally intelligent leaders [111] demonstrate higher productivity, lower turnover, and greater employee satisfaction. [112] Companies that invest in developing emotional intelligence [113] among their leadership teams [114] often see improvements in workplace culture and financial performance. [115] In our increasingly complex and interconnected world, [116] the importance of emotional intelligence in leadership [117] will only continue to grow. [118] Future leaders must cultivate this skill [119] in order to succeed [120] in building organizations that are both effective and humane. [121]

passages.title: Climate Change and Ocean Acidification
passages.text: Human activities, particularly the burning of fossil fuels, [122] have increased atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations [123] by more than 40 percent since the industrial revolution. [124] This escalating greenhouse gas buildup [125] drives global warming, which poses unprecedented challenges [126] to ecosystems and human societies worldwide. [127] Less well-known than global warming but equally alarming is ocean acidification, [128] a process by which carbon dioxide absorbed [129] by seawater reduces the ocean's pH level. [130] When carbon dioxide dissolves [131] in seawater, it forms carbonic acid that [132] lowers the ocean's alkalinity and makes it more acidic. [133] This chemical change threatens the survival of marine [134] organisms that depend on [135] calcium carbonate to build their shells and skeletons. [136] Pteropods, tiny marine snails that form [137] a crucial part of the ocean food chain, [138] are particularly vulnerable to ocean acidification. [139] As their shells dissolve in acidic water, [140] pteropods become less able to survive and reproduce. [141] The collapse of pteropod populations [142] would cascade through marine ecosystems, [143] threatening fish species and marine mammals that depend [144] on pteropods for nutrition. [145] Coral reefs, among the most biodiverse ecosystems on Earth, [146] face similar threats from both warming waters and acidification. [147] Warmer water causes corals to expel [148] their symbiotic algae, a process called bleaching [149] that leaves corals vulnerable to disease and death. [150] Ocean acidification further stresses corals [151] by making it difficult for them to build and maintain their calcium carbonate skeletons. [152] Beyond ecological impacts, ocean acidification [153] threatens human food security and economic livelihoods. [154] Millions of people worldwide depend [155] on seafood and fish for primary nutrition and income. [156] The disruption of marine food webs caused by [157] widespread ocean acidification [158] could result in severe economic consequences and food shortages [159] for vulnerable populations. [160] Addressing ocean acidification requires [161] reducing carbon dioxide emissions dramatically. [162] While mitigation strategies such as renewable energy development [163] are essential, [164] some scientists propose adaptation strategies, including [165] ocean alkalinity enhancement and selective breeding [166] of more resilient coral and shellfish species. [167] Comprehensive international action [168] combining emissions reduction with adaptation measures [169] represents the best hope for protecting our oceans [170] and the billions of people who depend on marine resources. [171]
